distillation_scope_note: Disease-specific medical input is limited to the disease name: Serotonin syndrome. Specific drug triggers, overdose, linezolid or MAOI context, opioid coexposure, stimulant exposure, severe hyperthermia, NMS mimicry, infection overlap, and rhabdomyolysis are represented only as axes, mechanisms, risk/context factors, event hazards, treatment modifiers, or case evidence.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Central and peripheral serotonin excess with 5-HT1A and 5-HT2A receptor overactivation after serotonergic exposure, interaction, dose escalation, impaired clearance, or overdose. This is the root disease activity and can fall quickly after short half-life drugs are stopped but persist with long half-life agents or MAO inhibition.

Spinal and brainstem serotonergic overactivity producing clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, myoclonus, inducible ankle clonus, rigidity, and incoordination. Lower-extremity predominance and clonus help distinguish this field from many mimics.
Serotonergic and catecholaminergic autonomic activation causing tachycardia, hypertension or labile pressure, tachypnea, diaphoresis, mydriasis, fever, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Mental status excitation and toxic encephalopathy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Serotonergic CNS toxicity causing agitation, anxiety, delirium, hallucinations, confusion, reduced GCS, coma, and seizure susceptibility. Sedatives and airway support reshape this mechanism without proving or excluding the disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Muscle heat generation and rhabdomyolysis cascade
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Sustained rigidity, clonus, tremor, agitation, seizures, and physical restraint generate heat, lactate, CK and myoglobin release, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and pigment nephropathy. Severe temperature elevation is muscle-driven and does not reliably respond to antipyretics.
Uncontrolled hyperthermia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, hypoxemia, aspiration, acidosis, DIC physiology, shock, and renal injury accumulate into respiratory failure, AKI, DIC, and death.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Serotonin syndrome requires exposure to one or more serotonergic agents, interactions, or serotonergic toxins.
Compatible timing clusters within hours to about one day after dose increase, new drug, interaction, or overdose, while long half-life agents can prolong activity.
Multiple serotonergic agents increase receptor agonism and interaction risk.
Large acute ingestion can saturate serotonergic pathways and prolong toxicity.
MAO inhibition, including linezolid-like context, reduces monoamine metabolism and can precipitate syndrome with serotonergic drugs.
Excess serotonin directly increases spinal motor neuron excitability.
Central and peripheral serotonergic activation drives autonomic hyperactivity.
CNS serotonergic toxicity changes arousal, attention, perception, and seizure threshold.
Clonus is a defining neuromuscular sign and may be spontaneous, inducible, or ocular.
Ocular clonus is a recognized serotonin toxicity sign.
Hyperreflexia commonly accompanies tremor and clonus, often more in lower limbs.
Resting, postural, or intention tremor reflects serotonergic motor overactivity.
Myoclonus can be spontaneous or inducible during moderate to severe toxicity.
Rigidity occurs in more severe syndrome and can mask clonus if extreme.
Fever and hyperthermia reflect autonomic and muscle activity.
Tachycardia is common in autonomic toxicity.
Hypertension or labile pressure can occur during sympathetic surge.
Tachypnea follows agitation, hyperthermia, acidosis, and respiratory stress.
Diaphoresis is a common autonomic sign and pairs with clonus in diagnostic criteria.
Mydriasis can appear with autonomic activation.
Peripheral serotonin increases gastrointestinal motility.
Agitation is a common mental status manifestation and worsens heat generation.
Confusion, delirium, hallucinations, reduced consciousness, and coma reflect CNS toxicity.
Seizures occur in severe toxicity or co-ingestion and amplify hyperthermia and acidosis.
Clonus, tremor, rigidity, and myoclonus generate heat and muscle injury when sustained.
Agitation, seizures, and restraint increase muscular heat and lactate.
Severe muscle-driven hyperthermia can rapidly injure organs.
Sustained muscle activity and adrenergic stress raise lactate.
Lactic acidosis and metabolic stress lower bicarbonate.
Rhabdomyolysis raises CK.
Muscle breakdown releases myoglobin and can worsen kidney injury.
Rhabdomyolysis and acidosis can produce hyperkalemia.
CK and myoglobin injury can cross into clinical rhabdomyolysis.
Myoglobinuria and hypovolemia increase AKI hazard.
Extreme hyperthermia can trigger coagulopathy and DIC physiology.
Observed seizure activity indicates ongoing seizure hazard and airway risk.
Aspiration, respiratory muscle stress, sedation, and ARDS can reduce oxygenation.
Coma, seizures, aspiration, hypoxemia, and severe acidosis can require ventilatory support.
Airway protection, deep sedation, paralysis, and respiratory failure can require intubation.
AKI from rhabdomyolysis, hypovolemia, shock, or nephrotoxin exposure raises creatinine.
Renal hypoperfusion, catabolism, or AKI raise BUN.
Muscle injury, hyperthermia, or hypoxic liver stress can increase AST.
Hepatic stress or co-ingestion can increase ALT.
Death is mediated by uncontrolled hyperthermia, seizures, AKI, DIC, respiratory failure, shock, aspiration, and severe co-ingestion.

axes.shape_free_text: Recent exposure to serotonergic drugs or toxins. This includes antidepressants, MAO inhibition context, linezolid-like exposure, serotonergic opioids, dextromethorphan, triptans, lithium, stimulants, supplements, or overdose; it is exposure evidence, not a diagnostic label.

Time from new serotonergic drug, dose increase, interacting drug addition, illicit exposure, or overdose to symptom snapshot. Values near 0-1 strongly fit rapid-onset serotonin toxicity, while long half-life drugs can prolong course.
Number of active serotonergic or serotonin-modulating agents at the relevant time, including prescribed drugs, over-the-counter agents, opioids, MAO inhibitors, and recreational substances.
Intentional or accidental large serotonergic ingestion or high exposure state.
MAO inhibition context from MAOI drugs or MAO-inhibiting antibiotics such as linezolid, increasing serotonin toxicity risk when combined with serotonergic agents.
Reduced metabolic or renal clearance, CYP interaction, advanced age, hepatic impairment, renal impairment, or long half-life drug accumulation that prolongs serotonergic activity.
Spontaneous or inducible clonus, often ankle/lower-extremity predominant. Use as a finding axis; ocular clonus can be additionally represented as a satellite.
Ocular clonus or rhythmic ocular oscillation in serotonin toxicity.
Brisk or pathologically increased tendon reflexes, often lower-extremity predominant.
Resting, postural, intention, or generalized tremor caused by neuromuscular hyperexcitability.
Spontaneous or inducible myoclonic jerks from serotonin toxicity; may overlap with clonus or seizure descriptions.
Increased muscle tone or rigidity, usually worse in severe serotonin syndrome. Extreme rigidity amplifies heat generation and can obscure clonus.
Psychomotor agitation, restlessness, anxiety, combativeness, or excitation in serotonin toxicity.
Confusion, delirium, hallucination, disorientation, coma, or reduced consciousness from toxic encephalopathy.
Level of consciousness measurement; low values indicate airway and ICU risk in severe toxicity or co-ingestion.
Witnessed seizure, convulsion, or recurrent seizure-like activity during toxicity.
Fever or severe hyperthermia. Temperatures above 40 C suggest severe muscle-driven toxicity and organ hazard.
Tachycardia from autonomic activation, fever, agitation, or acidosis.
Often elevated or labile during sympathetic surge; late hypotension should be interpreted through shock/complication axes rather than as core early serotonin activity.
Can be high or labile from autonomic activation; low MAP reflects complication physiology, sedation, shock, or co-ingestion rather than the core early syndrome.
Tachypnea from agitation, hyperthermia, acidosis, aspiration, or respiratory stress.
Usually preserved in uncomplicated syndrome but may fall with aspiration, coma, respiratory failure, sedatives, ARDS, or co-ingestion.
Diaphoresis or profuse sweating from autonomic activation.
Dilated pupils or reduced pupillary reactivity from autonomic toxicity or co-ingestion context.
Diarrhea or loose stools from peripheral serotonergic excess; vomiting/nausea may coexist but should use separate axes when needed.
May be normal or elevated from stress, infection overlap, seizure, or hyperthermia.
Rises with severe agitation, seizure, sustained muscle activity, hypoperfusion, or co-ingestion.
Low values reflect metabolic acidosis from lactate, seizure, renal injury, or co-ingestion.
Usually normal or mildly elevated in mild cases; can rise markedly with rigidity, clonus, seizure, hyperthermia, or rhabdomyolysis.
Rises with rhabdomyolysis and can precede or amplify AKI.
May rise with rhabdomyolysis, acidosis, renal impairment, or co-ingestion.
AKI from rhabdomyolysis, dehydration, hyperthermia, hypotension, or baseline renal disease.
Rises with renal hypoperfusion, dehydration, catabolism, or AKI.
Can rise with muscle injury, hyperthermia, hypoxic liver injury, or co-ingestion.
Can rise with hepatic injury, hyperthermia, shock, or co-ingestion.
Physical restraint or uncontrolled isometric activity during agitation. It can worsen hyperthermia and lactate and should not be modeled as treatment benefit.
Ability to deliver cyproheptadine orally or by nasogastric tube. Low values weaken cyproheptadine effect because no parenteral form is routinely available.
Need for deep sedation, intubation, paralysis, or ICU airway protection due to severe agitation, low GCS, seizure, respiratory failure, or extreme hyperthermia.
Daily hazard of uncontrolled muscle-driven hyperthermia causing organ injury, usually when temperature is above about 40 C with rigidity, clonus, agitation, or seizure.
Daily hazard of clinically important rhabdomyolysis from sustained neuromuscular activity, seizure, rigidity, hyperthermia, or restraint.
Daily hazard of seizure or recurrent seizure requiring urgent sedation/airway management.
Daily hazard of AKI from myoglobin, dehydration, hyperthermia, shock, or nephrotoxic/co-ingestion context.
Daily hazard of DIC-like coagulopathy in extreme hyperthermia, severe rhabdomyolysis, shock, or multiorgan injury.
Daily hazard of respiratory failure from coma, aspiration, severe acidosis, hypoxemia, ARDS, sedatives, or co-ingestion.
Daily hazard of intubation or ongoing invasive ventilation for airway protection, deep sedation/paralysis, respiratory failure, or severe neurologic toxicity.

Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from uncontrolled hyperthermia, seizure, rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, respiratory failure, shock, aspiration, and severe co-ingestion. Mild cases have very low hazard after prompt drug cessation.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Clonus and hyperreflexia are jointly driven by neuromuscular hyperexcitability.
Tremor plus hyperreflexia is a common diagnostic pairing.
Extreme temperature directly increases hyperthermia organ-injury hazard.
Rigidity increases heat generation and limits heat dissipation.
Restraint and isometric struggle raise lactate and heat.
High CK is the main lab correlate of rhabdomyolysis.
Myoglobin release causes pigment nephropathy risk.
Rhabdomyolysis transitions to AKI through myoglobin and volume depletion.
Extreme hyperthermia can produce DIC-like coagulopathy.
Seizures can cause aspiration, coma, or need for airway protection.
Ventilation requirement marks severe toxicity or co-ingestion and raises short-term mortality risk.
AKI reduces physiologic reserve and can require renal replacement therapy.
Uncontrolled hyperthermia is the central lethal pathway.
DIC contributes to bleeding, thrombosis, organ failure, and death.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Long half-life drugs, renal/hepatic impairment, or CYP interactions prolong toxicity after stopping agents.
MAO inhibition can prolong vulnerability and requires avoiding serotonergic re-challenge.

failure_modes: unrecognized long half-life or active metabolite
co-ingestion or infection contributing to toxicity

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Deep sedation can require airway monitoring or intubation.
Respiratory compromise changes benzodiazepine safety context.

side_effects.interpretation: Sedation can increase airway monitoring needs.
Respiratory depression can lower oxygen saturation in vulnerable patients.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe hyperthermia needs active cooling rather than antipyretic-only management.
Cooling alone is weaker if rigidity and clonus continue generating heat.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Extreme hyperthermia from rigidity may require paralysis plus active cooling.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rhabdomyolysis-associated AKI risk requires volume and urine-output support when tolerated.
Fluid strategy must avoid pulmonary edema when respiratory failure is active.

supportive_care: Preserve medication and toxin chronology exactly: agent list, dose change, overdose amount, interacting drug addition, and time from change to symptoms.

Use clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, myoclonus, rigidity, agitation, diaphoresis, diarrhea, fever, tachycardia, hypertension, lactate, CK, myoglobin, creatinine, potassium, and bicarbonate as ordinary ranking evidence when available.

Store Hunter criteria conclusion, final paper diagnosis, negative CT, negative cultures, NMS exclusion, and toxicology-consult agreement as confirmatory/context evidence with use_in_ranking:false when they are diagnostic conclusions rather than raw presentation findings.
Avoid antipyretic-only semantics for severe hyperthermia; temperature is driven by muscle activity and needs sedation, cooling, and sometimes paralysis.
Avoid physical restraint when possible because it increases heat and lactate; control agitation with benzodiazepines, sedation, and monitored care.

Trend vital signs, neurologic findings, CK, myoglobin, creatinine, urine output, electrolytes, bicarbonate, lactate, liver enzymes, coagulation studies, and respiratory status in moderate to severe toxicity.

Treat infection, NMS, anticholinergic toxicity, sympathomimetic toxicity, withdrawal, seizure disorder, and metabolic encephalopathy through their own evidence rather than deleting overlapping fever or mental-status data.

Escalate to ICU-level support for severe hyperthermia, rapidly rising CK/myoglobin, seizure, GCS depression, airway compromise, respiratory failure, severe acidosis, AKI, DIC, or unstable hemodynamics.
